grand_strategy.reading:
Ukraine runs a grand strategy of the weaker party that must make itself
indispensable to stronger ones: it cannot win the war outright, cannot
afford to lose it, and has to keep three patrons (the EU, the UK-led
coalition, the United States) paying while it negotiates with an adversary
whose price is its statehood. At the tactical level it is holding (the
front is slow in 2026, drones and strikes compensate for men), at the
theatre level it is trading minerals, drones and the promise of a rebuilt
country for money and guarantees, and at the grand-strategic level it is
betting that the road to the EU gives it an anchor that no ceasefire can
cancel. Luttwak's reversal is everywhere: the same logic that keeps the
patrons engaged (usefulness, visible strength, deep strikes, a national
story told in battle) irritates the neighbours whose vetoes decide the
anchor, from Fico's pipeline to Warsaw's history. 2026 is also the year the
centre of the question moved from the front to the table: talks opened
in Abu Dhabi in January, were frozen by the Iran war in March, and resumed
with the Miami round of 9-10 October, while the Kremlin still demands the
Donbas. Two signals that are not rows: the new Hungarian government's
shift from veto to conditions (Magyar, since May) and the Ankara
summit's quiet re-labelling of Ukraine as a contributor to Euro-Atlantic
security. Open question for the next review: whether the 15 Oct European
Council and the Miami outcome change the guarantee from a text to a force.
